provenance.method: lesson notes written from the NERDC 2025 scheme of work outline; every week keeps its scheme topic and bullets as the teaching spine

topics.title: The environment and us
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to state what an ecosystem is, list different habitats in Nigeria, explain how humans affect the environment, and identify ways to protect our surroundings.

Introduction:
We have learned about living and non-living things. Today we will see how these things interact in their homes called habitats.

Content:
An ecosystem is a community of living things interacting with their environment. In Nigeria, we have different habitats like forests, savannah, and wetlands. Humans affect the environment by building houses, farming, and throwing waste. When we cut down trees for firewood like many families do during harmattan season, we destroy animal homes. We can protect our environment by not burning bush, planting trees, and not throwing plastic naira wrappers on the ground.

Class activity:
Pupils will draw a Nigerian ecosystem and list three living things and three non-living things found there.

Evaluation questions:
What is an ecosystem? Name two habitats in Nigeria. How does burning bush affect the land? What can you do to protect your school environment?

Summary:
Our environment provides homes for plants and animals, and we must protect it for future generations.

topics.title: Water cycle and conservation
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to explain the water cycle, list ways water is used at home, identify ways water is wasted, and suggest methods to save water.

Introduction:
We use water every day for drinking, cooking, and cleaning. But where does this water come from and how can we make sure it never finishes?

Content:
The water cycle is how water moves from the ground to the sky and back again. Water evaporates from rivers like the Niger River, forms clouds, then falls as rain. In Nigeria, we use water for drinking, washing clothes, and farming. We waste water by leaving taps running while brushing teeth or using too much water to wash a single plate. To save water, we can fix leaking taps immediately, collect rainwater in drums during the rainy season, and use buckets instead of running water for bathing.

Class activity:
Pupils will conduct a water audit at home by counting how many times water taps are left running in one day.

Evaluation questions:
What happens to water when it evaporates? Name two ways we use water at home. How can you save water when taking a bath? Why should we fix leaking taps?

Summary:
Water is precious and we must all work together to conserve it for future use.

topics.title: Air and noise pollution
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to identify sources of air and noise pollution, explain their effects on health, suggest ways to reduce pollution, and conduct a simple pollution survey.

Introduction:
The air we breathe should be clean and the noise around us should not harm our ears. Today we will learn about things that make our air noisy and dirty.

Content:
Air pollution comes from things like old danfo buses that smoke too much, burning waste, and factories. When we breathe dirty air, we can cough, get asthma, or have chest pains. Noise pollution comes from generators, loud music, and construction work. Too much noise can damage our ears and make it hard to concentrate in class. To reduce pollution, we can walk to nearby places instead of taking bikes, play music at low volume, and report smoking vehicles to authorities.

Class activity:
Pupils will walk around the school and record sources of air and noise pollution on a chart.

Evaluation questions:
Name two sources of air pollution in Nigeria. How does dirty air affect our health? What makes too much noise? What can you do to reduce noise pollution?

Summary:
Clean air and quiet surroundings help us stay healthy and learn better in school.

topics.title: Waste management
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to explain what waste is, differentiate between biodegradable and non-biodegradable waste, list the three Rs of waste management, and create a recycling plan.

Introduction:
After we use things like food wrappers and sachet water, they become waste. Today we will learn how to handle waste properly.

Content:
Waste is anything we no longer need and throw away. Biodegradable waste like plantain peels and leftover food can break down naturally. Non-biodegradable waste like plastic bottles and nylon bags cannot break down easily and stay in the environment for many years. The three Rs of waste management are Reduce, Reuse, and Recycle. We can reduce waste by using our water bottles instead of buying new ones. We can reuse sachet bags as small bags for groundnuts. We can recycle paper by making new notepads from old ones.

Class activity:
Pupils will make a compost bin using biodegradable waste from the school kitchen.

Evaluation questions:
What is waste? Give an example of biodegradable waste. What do the three Rs stand for? How can you reuse a plastic bottle?

Summary:
Proper waste management keeps our environment clean and helps us live healthier lives.

topics.title: Climate and weather
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to differentiate between weather and climate, list weather instruments, explain how they work, and help set up a weather station.

Introduction:
Some days are hot and sunny, while other days are rainy and cool. We call these changes weather, but the pattern over many years is climate.

Content:
Weather is the condition of the atmosphere at a particular time and place, like today being hot and sunny. Climate is the average weather pattern in an area over many years, like Nigeria having two rainy seasons. Weather instruments help us measure weather conditions. A thermometer measures temperature in degrees Celsius. A rain gauge measures how much rain falls. A wind vane shows which direction the wind is blowing. We can make simple weather instruments using materials like a clear plastic bottle for a rain gauge and a cardboard arrow for a wind vane.

Class activity:
Pupils will help set up a class weather station and record the temperature and rainfall for one week.

Evaluation questions:
What is the difference between weather and climate? Name two weather instruments. How does a rain gauge work? What instrument shows wind direction?

Summary:
Weather instruments help us understand and predict changes in our environment.

topics.title: Bush burning and deforestation
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to explain what bush burning and deforestation are, list their effects on the land, identify ways to prevent them, and participate in planting a tree.

Introduction:
In some parts of Nigeria, people burn bushes to clear land for farming. Others cut down trees for firewood and building. These activities harm our environment.

Content:
Bush burning is setting fire to dry grass and bushes, often done to clear land quickly. Deforestation is cutting down trees faster than they can grow. These activities cause the soil to lose its nutrients, making it hard for plants to grow. They also destroy animal homes and lead to erosion. When trees are cut down, there is less rain and more flooding. We can prevent bush burning by using cutlass to clear land instead of fire. We can prevent deforestation by planting new trees when we cut old ones and using kerosene stoves instead of firewood for cooking.

Class activity:
Pupils will plant a tree seedling in the school compound and learn how to care for it.

Evaluation questions:
What is bush burning? How does deforestation affect animals? What happens to the soil after bush burning? How can we prevent deforestation?

Summary:
Trees are important for our environment and we must protect them from being destroyed.

topics.title: Erosion control
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to identify different types of erosion, explain their causes, suggest simple control methods, and participate in erosion control activities.

Introduction:
During the rainy season, we see water carrying away soil from some places. This is called erosion and it can damage farmlands and roads.

Content:
Erosion is the wearing away of soil by water or wind. There are different types of erosion. Sheet erosion happens when water removes a thin layer of soil over a large area. Gully erosion forms deep channels in the soil like the ones we see in some parts of the East. Rill erosion creates small streams on the surface. Erosion is caused by heavy rain, cutting down trees, and poor farming methods. To control erosion, we can plant grass and trees on bare land, build small barriers with stones to slow down water, and create drainage channels around buildings to direct water away.

Class activity:
Pupils will make simple erosion barriers using stones and soil in a small tray to demonstrate how they prevent soil loss.

Evaluation questions:
What is erosion? Name two types of erosion. What causes erosion? How can planting grass help control erosion?

Summary:
Erosion damages our land and we must use simple methods to control it and protect our environment.

topics.title: First aid and safety
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to list common injuries, explain basic first aid procedures, demonstrate emergency response, and participate in safety drills.

Introduction:
Accidents can happen anywhere, at home or at school. Knowing what to do in an emergency can save a life.

Content:
First aid is immediate help given to someone who is injured or suddenly sick. Common injuries include cuts, burns, and choking. For a cut, we should wash the wound with clean water, apply antiseptic, and cover with a bandage. For a small burn from hot water or fire, we should place the injured part under cold running water for 10 minutes. For choking, we should help the person lean forward and pat their back firmly. In emergencies, we should stay calm, call for adult help, and not move someone who might have a neck injury. We should also know the emergency numbers like 112 and the location of the nearest hospital.

Class activity:
Pupils will practice basic first aid procedures on dolls and participate in an earthquake drill.

Evaluation questions:
What is first aid? What should you do for a small cut? How do you help someone who is choking? What number should you call in an emergency?

Summary:
Knowing first aid helps us help others during accidents and emergencies.

topics.title: Science and careers
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to list science-related careers in Nigeria, explain the importance of science in these careers, identify their own career interests, and present their career dreams.

Introduction:
The things we learn in science class can help us do many different jobs when we grow up. Science is used in almost every profession.

Content:
In Nigeria, there are many science-related careers. A doctor uses science to understand how the body works and treat illnesses. An engineer uses science to build roads, bridges, and buildings like the Third Mainland Bridge. An agricultural scientist uses science to improve crop yields and develop new farming methods. A computer programmer uses science to create apps and websites. Science helps these professionals solve problems and make new discoveries. To pursue a science career, we should study hard, especially in mathematics and science subjects, and ask questions about how things work.

Class activity:
Pupils will research and present on a science career they are interested in pursuing.

Evaluation questions:
Name three science-related careers. How does a doctor use science? Why is science important for engineers? What science subject do you like most and why?

Summary:
Science opens many career opportunities and helps us understand and improve our world.

topics.title: Revision and science fair
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to recall key concepts learned throughout the term, demonstrate understanding through practical projects, present their work clearly, and ask questions about peers' projects.

Introduction:
Today we will review what we have learned this term and share the science projects we have been working on.

Content:
This term we have learned about the environment, water cycle, pollution, waste management, weather, erosion, first aid, and science careers. A science fair is a place to show what we know and have created. For our science fair, each pupil has made a project showing something they learned. Some have made models of the water cycle, others have shown ways to reduce waste, and some have demonstrated first aid procedures. When presenting, we should speak clearly, explain how our project works, and answer questions from teachers and classmates.

Class activity:
Pupils will set up their science projects around the classroom and take turns presenting to their classmates.

Evaluation questions:
What is one thing you learned about the environment? How does the water cycle work? Why is it important to reduce waste? What science career interests you most?

Summary:
The science fair helps us show what we have learned and develop our presentation skills.
